Marty Napoleon

Pianist Marty Napoleon was born in New York on June 2, 1921. He was working steadily in jazz by his early twenties, performing with Chico Marx, Joe Venuti and Charlie Barnet. Marty had the opportunity to work with his uncle Phil in the Memphis Five and with his brother Teddy in a piano quartet. He toured and recorded with Louis Armstrong, Gene Krupa, Red Allen and led his own piano trio. A lifelong resident of New York, he continues to perform and share his wealth of jazz lore.
Marty was interviewed in New York City on January 15, 1999, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.

We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. My name is Monk Rowe and we are in Manhattan, and I’m very pleased to have Marty Napoleon with me today, who is a jazz pianist with a long and successful career, and I just learned quite a collector and annotator of your own career too. So welcome.
Thank you, Monk. It’s a pleasure to meet you.
You seem to have a lot of enjoyment in your career in that you’ve saved all this material, and you’re very proud of your travels.

Oh yes. Well a funny thing is about my traveling and about my performances as a piano player, people have often asked me after a concert, they would come up to me, or during concerts on the break or something and say, “Are you really having that much fun, or are you just doing that for cameras and stuff?” I say, “well let me ask you a question. What would you like to do more than anything else in the world? What’s your favorite hobby?” And somebody would say baseball or football, golf. So say they say, “I like to golf.” I say, “okay, all right, you like to golf? Do you love it with all your heart?” “Yeah, I guess so.” “Well suppose you went out golfing every day of your life, and you got paid for it.” It’s like the baseball players, right? These guys, they love to play baseball, they go out and they get paid. Golfers love to golf and they get paid for it. I play the piano. And I’m so lucky to have people pay me for what I’m playing. I mean come on. Why shouldn’t I be happy up there, I love it, it’s great, I’m having a ball.
Can you recall at what age did you think you could actually make a career as a musician? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

I recall every day of my life just about, I swear, all of it. Really. I remember asking my mother a question once, where I said, “Mom, you remember when you were scrubbing the floor in the kitchen?” And she uttered some obscenity about some neighbors or somebody, and I said, “were you talking about me?” She said, “no, honey, not you, no, no, I mean them.” So I said, “how old was I then?” She says, “you were two years old.” And after that she says, “I thought you were going to be a school teacher because I used to stand up and by the time I was three or four years old I used to stand on the chair by the kitchen table, and bang the table, and speak gibberish. She thought I was making speeches, which I was, I was making speeches and banging my fist on the table. So I remember all of these crazy little things you know. But as far as being a musician or a piano player, well the fact is that when I was about seven or eight years old I had a brother who was like four or five years older than I, and he was kind of like a Danny Kaye kind of character, he was crazy, he was like a nut job. He’d do all these crazy motions. And he used to sing like comedy songs. And I used to sing harmony to him. And my father, who was a banjo player, said, “this kid’s got a great ear.” And I had a good ear, because I could hear harmonies at the time I was about seven years old. And when I used to go to grammar school, we’d sit in the auditorium and they’d say “everybody stand up, we’re going to sing the ‘Star Spangled Banner’” and the kids would be singing [sings] Oh say can you see—and I was singing [sings harmony] Oh say can you see, by the dawn’s early light. And the kid next to me says, “hey, you’re singing it wrong.” I says, “shut up, I know what I’m doing.” I was singing counterharmonies. I mean this is what I heard. And the funny thing is, to jump ahead of myself, when I was with the Chico Marx band, one of my first big bands, actually there was band before that was my first big band, but Chico Marx was my first name big band. And we played, you know Chico Marx, the Marx Brothers, and I was on the road with that band for a year and a half. My wife, we had just gotten married and we were on the road, and we were doing mostly only theaters, mostly theaters anyway, and we’d have, each week we were in a different town, and we’d have an eight o’clock rehearsal in the theater and they’d have people like Larry Adler, who is my biggest nightmare because he was playing all these “Rhapsody in Blue” and Ravel’s “Bolero” and I couldn’t read note one. So I was faking everything. In fact the first band I was with was a guy named Bob Astor’s band, and we © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

had a kid on trumpet named Neal Hefti, who was writing arrangements for the band, and Bob would say every Monday he had to bring in an arrangement for Tuesday rehearsal see, or Monday rehearsal, whatever. And during the week he’d say “Neal, how are you doing with the arrangement?” Neal would say “you’ll have it in time, don’t worry.” Came Monday for the rehearsal, he never got to the rhythm section. He wouldn’t finish the arrangement, because he couldn’t write a score.
Oh, he just wrote the parts individually.

What he did was, Neal Hefti was rooming with Shelly Manne the drummer. And Shelly used to complain because Neal didn’t know how to write a score, so he would whistle the arrangement, the entire arrangement from the introduction, chorus, modulation, out choruses, background choruses, everything he would whistle, each part, and after he finished the lead trumpet he would throw it on the floor and look at it, and harmonize it. [Whistles] He was whistling all night long, and Shelly used to call him “the whistler” — he said, “he drove me crazy,” in fact at night he’d have all these parts on the floor and I would get up to go to the bathroom and he’d say “watch it, Shelly, you’re stepping on my baritone.” He says I felt like I was walking through a cow pasture there. It was unbelievable. And Neal and I were one day coming down in an elevator in the hotel going to work, and he said to me you know what my biggest thrill would be in life? My ambition, that’s what he said, “my ambition is to someday write for the Count Basie Orchestra.” Do you think he achieved his goal?
I guess so. You know it might have been an advantage for you that he didn’t get to the piano part, because he might have written something very difficult, if you weren’t a reader at the time.

Well actually what happened was he would pass out the parts at the rehearsals see, and the bass player’s name was Marty too. See? Well he was Marty Two, I was Marty One, and Shelly was the drummer, and he would give us blank manuscripts and he would say “Shelly, Marty Bass and Marty Piano.” The only reason we knew it was piano was because in the left hand side it said “Piano,” and the manuscript was empty. And I’d say “hey Neal, when are you going to write me a part? I’m trying to learn how to read music.” So anyway, to get back to Chico, I couldn’t read. I hadn’t learned yet, because I was like scuffling. So when we got to Chico’s band and I was like playing these shows © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

with comedians and dancers, I was lucky that we had an 18 piece orchestra. And fortunately I had what they called a piano/conductor part. And on the top, in red ink, was what the lead trumpet was playing, see? So now I would fake through the first show and from the second show on I would follow the red notes on the piano sheets see? And I would notice like whenever the band had an eighth rest and a dotted quarter, I know it always went [scats] and I said, hey that’s great, you know. By the time I left that band I was reading music.
That’s fascinating. And that must have been standard procedure for those arrangers back then to put the trumpet part in red?

Well no it wasn’t that, it was the people who had the act, like the dance team or the comedian or the harmonica player, whoever, they would hand out their parts. It wasn’t the orchestra parts, it was the parts from the act that we were playing.
I see.

Because when they didn’t know they would say well this is the drummer’s part, and this is the saxophone players, and this is the piano/conductor, because the piano player was usually the conductor. And they would say piano/conductor. So I was lucky because all of those things had those red lines, those red music dots on there, and that’s how I learned how to read. In fact the funny thing was, only about three years ago, my wife and I were sitting in the living room and I said, “well you know I scuffled during Chico’s band because I couldn’t read.” She said, “you didn’t know how to read when you were with Chico’s band?” She never even knew I couldn’t read. Because we were too busy, we had just gotten married, we were busy doing something else.
And that was what year?
1942, February. I joined them February of ’42.
Now you having come from a musical family—
Exactly.
—can I assume that it was okay with your parents that you were going into this field?

As a matter of fact that’s funny you lead me into that. Because when I started going with my wife, I met my wife when we were both 18 years old. Obviously we were the same age just about. And we kept company for about two years. But after about a year, my father said to me “you can’t keep company with that girl.” I said, “why not?” He says, © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

“you’re planning on marrying her?” I said, “yeah.” He said, “well you can’t even think about that.” I said, “why?” He said, “she’s going to keep you away from studying the piano.” How would you like to have parents like that?
Wow. That’s a turnaround.
Well see you talk about a musical family?
Really.

My father played banjo and guitar, my mother played guitar, I had two brothers and two sisters. My brother Teddy was a piano player, my brother Andy was a drummer, both of my sisters were singers. My sister Margaret married a piano player named Shorty Allen, and my sister Josephine married a saxophone player named Bill Shine. Fantastic lead alto man. And my grandfather, my father’s father, played guitar, and my aunt — he was living with his daughter Josephine until he died, and she says the day he died he was sitting with the guitar in his hand, strumming the guitar. And then his father played guitar. So it went way back with the guitars and the music. And everybody, in fact when I started this project with the book, people used to say to me, “how many musicians in your generation, your family are musically inclined, or jazz or whatever.” I’d say, “I don’t know.” I started counting them and I got to 50 and I lost count. Because not only my family, but my mother’s side.
Well your uncle—
Phil. Right.
Trumpet.

See the thing, to start it off this way, I usually start off my interviews by saying my father was the oldest of five brothers and one sister. All of the boys were professional musicians. And my father was the oldest, and he played banjo and guitar, my uncle Georgie, George Napoleon played the saxophone, my uncle Teddy was a drummer, my uncle Joey was a saxophone player — and who else, there were five brothers — Pop, Georgie, Teddy, Joey—
And Phil?

And Phil, right, I forgot. All musicians. Now before my uncle Phil Napoleon passed away, he called me about once every week and a half or two weeks, like that. He would call me because he wanted me to have the cemetery plots, he wanted to leave them to me © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

because I was the last surviving Napoleon on his side. And he would tell me stories about my father. And he said, “you know when your father was about 18 years old, 19, 18, he bought a trumpet because he wanted to play the trumpet. And he started a jazz club like I forget the name of it now, he told me what the name is I can’t remember, the Arrowsmith or the Arrow Club. And they used to chip in dues to belong to this jazz club, it was a club, you know, a society? And he said he used to put the trumpet in a closet on one of the shelves, and Phil was about five years old and he found the trumpet one day. And he started fooling with it. Next thing he was getting sounds, and my father caught him one day playing, about a year later, and he says, “I’m going to switch to guitar,” he says, or banjo, because he says, “I could never do what you’re doing.” And he was five years old. So what happened was my father used to do dates, and he would bring Phil with him on the job, at five years old. And during the course of the evening he would make an announcement about his kid brother, and put a chair in the middle of the floor, and put him on that chair and he would play the trumpet. People went absolutely bananas.
Wow. The little Mozart.
Yeah, he was great.
Well your career started when the big bands were pretty healthy.
Right.
And you obviously did marry your wife.
Obviously.
Well it’s stood the test of time anyway.

Oh boy I’m telling you. And then we went back to my mother’s house after we got married, she lived a block away, and we had a sandwich and a glass of milk and my wife walked me to the subway, and I went back to Pennsylvania, and I finished two weeks with the band, and I did my honeymoon alone in Buffalo. I said, “man, nobody’s had a honeymoon like this.” I spent my honeymoon alone man.
In Buffalo.
In Buffalo.
In the winter.
It’s cold.
My God. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

It was cold. I can’t believe how cold it gets in Buffalo. And anyway, that’s what happened. So listen to this, now here’s another funny story. I get back to New York and now we’re married, so we check into the Forrest Hotel, and the band that I was with has some time off, so we get married and we checked into the Forrest Hotel on 48th Street in New York, and about three o’clock in the morning the phone rings. Four o’clock in the morning. And I can’t even find the phone, it’s like on the floor or something. I said, “hello?” “Who’s this?” “Marty, this is Shelly Manne.” I says, “what’s happening, Shelly?” He says, “we’re having a jam session at the Capitol Hotel in the ballroom.” I says, “I’ll be right there.” So I hung up the phone, and my wife says, “where you going?” I says, “Shelly said they’re having a session.” So she says, “you’re not going without me.” So we got our clothes on, we went over there, and about 30 years later I’m doing a club date, a Jewish wedding someplace, and the drummer was a club date leader. He says, “Marty, do you know when you got married you went to a jam session at the Capitol Hotel.” I said, “how’d you know that?” He says, “I was playing drums.” And he says, “you know what? I looked over and your wife was sitting in the corner by you on the piano, falling asleep.” He says, “how dare you?” And my wife says, “yeah, if I knew he was going to do that, that would have been it, that would have been it.”
You know I think some script writer must have known about that because that’s the scene in the Glenn Miller story in the movie.
Oh yeah?
He gets married, he goes back to the hotel and all the guys show up at this thing and they go down and they hear Louis Armstrong.

I’ve got a picture here of that, when we did that scene. I’ve got a picture in the book. It was strange, I’ll tell you. But it was great, and funny, when I did get married, and I told my father we got married and he gave me a can opener. He said, “here, you’re going to need this?” I said, “what are you kidding? My wife’s going to be a great cook.” Because she had never cooked before. She was a dressmaker and she used to go to work every day, and she used to come home and her mother had dinner for her see? He says to me “here. You’re going to need this.” And she says, “how dare your father, he said I was going to need a can opener?” So we went on the road, and instead of staying in hotels, there was a trombone player named Chuck Maxon with Chico Marx’s band. He and his © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

wife were married ten years, and he was old hand at being on the road. So we kind of hung out because his wife and my wife became very good friends. And she’d say, “don’t stay in the hotel,” the whole band would go in the hotel — he’d say we won’t stay in the hotel, we’ll stay in hotels with — what do they call them, kitchenettes. You know because we’re going to be in each town for a week. So rather than just spend rent money, we could cook and you’d save some money. And my wife learned how to cook that way. It was great, I loved it. It was just a fascinating story. And people ask me these questions all the time about my life on the road. When I tell them these stories, my wife says, “you’re a blabbermouth” because I never stop. I say “I can’t help it, I just love it.” I love talking about it because everybody’s fascinated by what we went through. I mean there are stories that are incredible.
Did it get to the point where you had had enough of it?
Never.
Never.

Oh until now. The only reason I don’t work as much as I did now is my wife isn’t feeling well. So I decided hey, I’ve been on the road over 50 years and she’s waiting for me all this time, now I’m going to spend some time with her, and that’s why I carry my phone with me all the time, to keep track of her. My daughter’s calling, keep track, she’s got her girlfriend sitting with her. She’s not well at all.
Well you have played with an amazing list of people.
Did you see that list I gave you?
Yes, I’m looking at it now. I have my own little sheet here too.
Oh you have your own thing, I see.
Joe Venuti? Some really marvelous — not only musicians but characters.
Joe Venuti himself was a character. Unbelievable. I was telling a story just the other day about Joe Venuti. We played Palisades Park. Do you remember that name at all?
Sure.

Palisades Park? Well when we played Palisades Park in New Jersey, Cliffside, someplace, and we used to do on Saturdays a matinee, and right across the park was an Italian restaurant. And we’d go there for dinner. And Joe knew the bosses, which didn’t matter anyway, but we would sit there and he would tell us stories, and we did more © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

laughing than eating because he was a very funny guy. There were stories about Joe Venuti that you don’t believe, and I’ve got some in my book that are incredible. About one where we were working at a park in Lincoln, not Nebraska, Lincoln Park in Massachusetts someplace, Bedford, Mass. Anyway, it was an outdoor park, it was an amusement park, and it was September and we were freezing. Guys were wearing overcoats and gloves. I was playing piano with gloves on, so was Joe.
Joe, with the violin.

No he took a chair and he broke it up and he said to the band, “go buy some weenies,” and the kid went to the store to buy the weenies and he came back and Joe took the chair and broke it up and built a fire on the bandstand. Then he took the weenies like this and he was sitting there while the band was playing and the kids were dancing, and he was roasting hot dogs, see? And the manager came running, and was furious. Because the kids, instead of dancing, they came around to watch the band. He says, “what the hell is this guy doing?” He’s cooking frankfurters. So the manager went crazy. He says, “what are you doing? Well Joe was very cool you know, and he used to look at you this way and bite his lip saying, “what’s wrong, whatsa matter?” The guy says, “what’s wrong? You’ve got a fire on the bandstand.” He says, “well the guys are freezing man, I’m trying to feed them, because we’re cold.” So he says, “you broke my chair.” Joe he got up and put his hand up and says, “how much was the chair?” He was going to pay for the chair. He was crazy. But he had such great stories, I’m telling you. I’ve got some stories in my book about him you won’t believe. You just don’t believe man.
When was your first opportunity to record?

I think the first, well the first professional record date I did was I was working at Childs’ Paramount Restaurant on Broadway and 43rd Street. It was downstairs from the Paramount Theater. Do you remember the Paramount Theater where Frank Sinatra had that whole thing with the bobby soxers? There was a restaurant downstairs called Childs’ Paramount, and I was working with Henry’s band, and I got a call from a guy named Teddy Reig, who was a, did you know that name?
Yeah, a big producer. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Savoy Records, Guild Records, whatever. And he called me and my first record date was, are you ready for this? My first record date, Kay [sic] Winding, or Kai as he was known later, Shelly Manne, Ed Safranski, and Allen, boy, I just drew a blank.
Sax player? Allen Eager?

Yes. How did you know that? Well you should know that. And Allen Eager. And what happened was the gig became a fiasco, I hate to say this, but because of Allen Eager. Because he was like a negative personality. Because Kai would say “hey what are we going to play? How about —” And the guys were making suggestions. Like why don’t we play this, why don’t we play this. Everything was said, Allen would say “no man, don’t play that.” So we tried to please him and say “all right we’ll play that.” Nobody really wanted to play the tunes he wanted, but they were trying to appease him. And everybody wound up like this. And I did a three hour interview for Phil Schaap on WKCR. And he played two of those records. I said, “I thought there was only one, called ‘Olgamore.’” He said, “no, there’s another one.” And I listened to it and I said now I know why I don’t have the other one. It’s terrible. You know it was the beginning of the bebop thing and everybody is [scats], with flatted fifths and all that. And it was really terrible. I mean you’ve got great musicians like this. But it wasn’t very good. Plus the fact that there was so much tension at that date. We went in at about one o’clock in the morning and we played until about twelve noon the next day, and they only put that one record out, two sides or whatever it was, and we never got paid for the overtime. So I saw Teddy Reig about 30 years later, I says, “hey Teddy, you know I never got any overtime for that date?” He says, “here, here’s ten dollars.” He gave me ten dollars out of his pocket.
Well it’s interesting that a lot of recording at that time must have been pretty much off the cuff. You get the musicians together and then you decide what you’re going to play.

Oh that’s what it was. So everything was mostly head arrangements, that’s how they started those heads. But the thing was, what was bad about it was the promoters, who knew nothing about music, but they just happened to know the musicians, they would get them in the studio and they would say “just make something up.” And they would make something up and then somebody would come up with a name for the song, and the guys © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
would never get any royalties for it. So now there’s a couple of guys, friends of mine now, they’re let me see, Dean Pratt and Don Sickler. Do you know those names?
Don Sickler I recognize.

Don Sickler is a publisher and he’s got this music composer’s something, and they look out for royalties for musicians who’ve been getting screwed over the years, not getting their just desserts. And they’re beautiful, because they look out for musicians and make sure they get what they’re supposed to get you see? So that’s what happened. A lot of those little things where the guys made up a little head arrangement and nobody ever saw any money for it, except the guy who was running the record company.
What would a record date like that pay?
In those days, for a three hour session, forty-one and a quarter. $41.25.
You do have a pretty good memory.
I remember everything, I swear.
How about when you were first married and you were on the road? What kind of salary were you getting?

Well that’s a long story. You see when I left Bob Astor’s band, before I left Bob Astor’s band we were working in Youngstown, Ohio at the Elms Ballroom. And we were there for four weeks. And there was a local theater where bands used to come in and play, and what’s his name, Ray McKinley and Wilbur, the trombone player, now the age is catching me. Ray McKinley and Will Bradley, Bradley-McKinley, you know, 18th and Chestnut, between 18th and 19th on whatever, you know. Anyway, they came into town. They were thinking of splitting up. So I told Will Bradley, Will Bradley came to the Elms Ballroom and he heard us play and he flipped out. And he took some of us on the side on one of the breaks and he said, “you know Ray McKinley and I are breaking up,” and he says, “you guys are great, and I’m starting a new band and I’d love to have you guys with me.” And we said, “yeah,” because we were like young kids, it was the first band. You get an offer from a guy like Will Bradley, you say “I’m ready, I’m ready.” So what happened, we went back to New York, the band had some time off, we went back to New York and I went to the rehearsal. And now the piano player with Will Bradley’s band was a fellow named Billy Maxted. He wrote all the arrangements. In fact he wrote the arrangements with Chico Marx’s band see? So he wrote the arrangements for Bradley’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

band, and when Bradley wanted us to join his band, most of the guys with Astor’s band went with him, including me, but the thing was that Billy Maxted, when I went to the rehearsal he was playing piano and he says, “I’m not leaving the band until I get my money, because he owes me a lot of money for arrangements, see, and when I get my money I’ll call you, and you take my place.” I says okay. So in the meantime I used to go to Local 802. First we’d go to Local 802 to look for jobs, and then we would go to Nola Studios, where all the musicians used to hang out. And Nola Studios, did you ever hear of that name? Nola Studios? It was on Broadway and 52nd Street, 51st Street, upstairs where now there’s a hair, they teach girls how to make hair, whatever. And this place was huge. It was the whole floor, from 51st to 52nd Street, they had about twelve different studios, rehearsal studios. Every band that came into town rehearsed at Nola Studios. Bands would come into town— And every room had a door with a mail slot in it. So we would go up there if somebody was rehearsing, we’d look in the mail slot to see who was rehearsing, and try and sneak in and listen to the band. So I came up there one day and there was a girl receptionist, Ella Jean, and I said, “hey Ella Jean, who’s rehearsing today?” So I heard this music as I got out of the elevator, a big band coming from that room. And I said, “who’s in that room, the band sounds great.” She said, “Chico Marx.” I said, “the Marx Brothers?” She said, “no not the Marx brothers, just Chico, the piano player.” I said, “oh that’s great.” So I went over to the door to peek in the door to see what I could see. And as I went to open the slot, the door opened and somebody walked out and I snuck in. So I closed the door quietly and as I’m standing there, somebody in the band says, “hey Benny, there he is now.” And the whole band is looking at me. And there’s nobody in the room but the orchestra and me. So I gave it the old classic, “who, me?” So this guy comes over to me and he says, “hey, are you Marty Napoleon?” I said, “yeah, how did you know that?” He said, “we called your house, your wife said you went to the union.” I said, “yeah I was at the union and I just came over here to see who was rehearsing.” I said, “who are you?” He says, “I’m Ben Pollack, I’m the manager of the Chico Marx band.” He says, “would you like to try out for the band?” I says, “what?” Because see he called Maxted, because the piano player gave his notice. Benny called Billy Maxted. Maxted said, “call this kid” because he had my number. He said, “call him” so he called my house and my wife said, “he went to the union.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
And then you walked in the door.
And I walked in the door.
That’s really weird.

I’m telling you, there are fantastic stories. So he says, “would you like to try out?” Now I’d just left Bob Astor’s band where I couldn’t read this many notes. You know I didn’t know how to read music. So I went over, and he says, “do you want to try out?” I says, “yeah.” I couldn’t remember, everything was a blur. I didn’t remember seeing guys sitting in the band, nothing. All I saw was a piano and music, when they put the music out, and it had real chords written out. It didn’t have—
No symbols?

No symbols. It had real chords, like charts with chords. So when I sat down I just blacked out. I looked at that and I said forget it, it’s not going to happen. But since I had such a good ear from the time I was like six years old or whatever, or from birth, the band started to play and I played along with them. Now I found out later — first Benny comes over to me after I’d played a few numbers with the band, and he says, “okay, kid, you got the job.” And I’m saying why would this guy hire me? I mean I couldn’t hardly play, I couldn’t read, I didn’t know anything. He says, “You got the job. You get 75 bucks a week and we leave Monday for Philadelphia.” So I called my wife and I said, “Honey, quit your job, we’re going on the road.” She says, “get out of here, what are you talking about?” So I told her what happened. She said, “I don’t believe it. What are you talking about?” You know why she was incredulous? Well then let’s go. Okay.
Well hold on for a second.
Oh you want to look at them things.
Very quickly, what’s your take on the state of jazz today?

Jazz is alive I love it. There’s nothing wrong with jazz, it’s just we’re not getting enough exposure to the people. Because not enough radio stations play it, and like you get KCR and BGO, they’re playing some far out jazz that a lot of people don’t really like to listen to. So that’s my personal feeling. Because sometimes I listen to those stations and I don’t really like what I hear. Because I’m from the old jazz, you know, like Bunny Berigan, guys like this. And I love jazz, but when I listen to some of those things, you know when they do these free for all things, it just turns me off, I just don’t like it. So I feel if I don’t like it and I’m a musician, can you imagine the average lay person who listens and says what the hell is that?
Yeah, what are they doing?

Yeah, what is that? So I feel sad because you know how I know there’s a market for it? I went to Europe about five years in a row with Peanuts Hucko. We were doing a tribute to Louis Armstrong. segments.title: Opening and Marty's love of playing
segments.summary: Monk Rowe opens the filmed interview; Marty says he is lucky to be paid for something he loves.

segments.title: Early ear and singing harmony as a child
segments.summary: Marty recalls childhood, his comic brother, his banjo-playing father noting his ear, and singing harmony in school.

segments.title: Neal Hefti's whistled arrangements in Bob Astor's band
segments.summary: In Astor's band Neal Hefti whistled arrangements and handed out blank parts.

segments.title: Learning to read from the red notes in Chico's piano part
segments.summary: The red-ink trumpet lines in piano/conductor parts taught him to read; he joined Chico in February 1942.

segments.title: His wife, his father's objection, and the musical family
segments.summary: His father warns that marriage will keep him from piano; Marty lists his musically gifted relatives.

segments.title: The Napoleon brothers and Uncle Phil as a child trumpeter
segments.summary: Marty's father and uncles were all musicians, and he tells how young Phil found his father's trumpet.

segments.title: Honeymoon alone in Buffalo and the jam session after the wedding
segments.summary: Marty finished two weeks with the band after marrying, then went to a 4 a.m. jam at the Capitol Hotel.

segments.title: The can opener, cooking on the road, and never tiring of travel
segments.summary: His father gave him a can opener; kitchenettes on the Chico tour; he now stays closer to his ailing wife.

segments.title: Joe Venuti stories at Palisades Park and the bandstand fire
segments.summary: Marty recalls Joe Venuti as a character, including a fire built on the bandstand to roast hot dogs.

segments.title: First record date with Kai Winding, Shelly Manne and Allen Eager
segments.summary: His first professional date, arranged by Teddy Reig, was tense because of Allen Eager and ran overnight.

segments.title: Head arrangements, lost royalties and the $41.25 session fee
segments.summary: Early sessions used made-up heads whose players never got royalties; Marty remembers the scale pay.

segments.title: Will Bradley's offer, Nola Studios and sneaking into Chico's rehearsal
segments.summary: Will Bradley invited Astor's band to join him; Marty waited for the Maxted chair, haunted Nola Studios and walked in on Chico Marx's band.

segments.title: Hired by Ben Pollack at $75 a week
segments.summary: Pollack hires Marty despite his poor reading; his wife quits her job and joins him on the road.

segments.title: Teddy Powell's band, Charlie Ventura and Marty's brother Teddy
segments.summary: Marty recounts Teddy Powell's band, Ventura leaving for Krupa, recommending his brother, and quitting Powell.

segments.title: Joining Charlie Barnet's band through Jimmy Lamar
segments.summary: After reading about Barnet's band in Down Beat, Marty got a call for the Strand Theater job.

segments.title: Big-band audiences then and music today
segments.summary: Marty contrasts young audiences for melodic big-band music with rap; Monk offers a theory about rhythm.

segments.title: Union rules about quitting a band
segments.summary: Discussion of giving two weeks' notice and Marty paying his own fare from Toronto.

segments.title: Musicians in Teddy Powell's band and waltz sets in Boston
segments.summary: Boots Mussulli, Pete Condoli and others in Powell's band; playing waltz sets in Boston.

segments.title: The war's end and taking his family west with Barnet
segments.summary: Marty was not political; he was with Barnet at war's end and took his wife and baby daughter to California.

segments.title: Sitting in with Uncle Phil at Nick's and taking the job
segments.summary: Marty played Dixieland with Phil at Nick's, surprised him with a bop solo, and got the job.

segments.title: Tony Spargo, Bob Carter and Phil's complaint about swing playing
segments.summary: Sidemen in Phil's Memphis Five, bassist Bob Carter regaining sight, and Phil objecting to four/four swing.

segments.title: Writing his book, bebop influences and Erroll Garner
segments.summary: Marty mentions his unpublished book, favourite pianists Peterson and Garner, and Garner's intro on 'That's My Kick'.

segments.title: The bootleg Milan album with Louis and Tyree Glenn
segments.summary: A black-market double album of Marty and Tyree Glenn with Louis Armstrong, perhaps because both took encores.

segments.title: Replacing his brother Teddy in Gene Krupa's band
segments.summary: Marty sat in at the 400 Club, was offered Krupa's job when his brother had left, and went to California for films.

segments.title: Leaving Louis before 'High Society' and his 27 bags
segments.summary: He quit Louis' band from travel fatigue and missed 'High Society'; stolen luggage and Louis' 27 bags.

segments.title: Louis and Joe Glaser
segments.summary: Louis' priorities were his horn, Glaser and Lucille; Glaser made deals for other acts.

segments.title: Joe Glaser's call and the pitch to join Louis
segments.summary: Marty refused at first because of his vow to his wife; Red Norvo urged him on and he accepted.

segments.title: Loving music but hating the music business and the road
segments.summary: Marty distinguishes music from the business, recalls jam sessions, and tells how bus reading hurt his eyes.

segments.title: First European tour in 1952-53, Sweden and a demanding promoter
segments.summary: Overseas with Louis: a town that closed for the concert, then a German promoter rushing the band.

segments.title: Threats from Texas men and first encounters with Jim Crow
segments.summary: A confrontation outside a Texas club, then restaurants and water fountains in the South.

segments.title: Austin ballroom applause and a dangerous Florida hall
segments.summary: Hungry stop on a broken-down bus, a standing ovation in Austin, and a West Palm Beach hall with the stand raised high.

segments.title: Years at the Metropole with Shavers, Hawkins and others
segments.summary: Marty's ten years at the Metropole with Charlie Shavers and Coleman Hawkins.

segments.title: Country club dates and Art Ford's TV show
segments.summary: Tony Cabot society dates, and Marty's weeks on Art Ford's show ending over hiring advice.

segments.title: The Napoleon Brothers piano quartet and the Sands Hotel booking
segments.summary: Marty and Teddy formed a two-piano group, were booked via Jack Entrada, and clashed with the pit boss in the lounge.

segments.title: Louis Jordan's advice, Columbus, the group's end and rejoining Louis in 1966
segments.summary: The Columbus run, the group's decline, Marty quitting Louis for his children, and returning in 1966 for Jones Beach.

segments.title: Wrapping up and promising a second session
segments.summary: Monk suggests a Part Two; they note the time and turn to Marty's materials.

segments.title: State of jazz today and a European tour with Peanuts Hucko
segments.summary: Marty feels jazz needs exposure and tells of a Portuguese audience that cheered the Hucko Armstrong tribute band.

segments.title: Looking through Marty's photographs and goodbyes
segments.summary: Marty shows family photos and pictures of Astor, Manne and Chico Marx, and the interview ends.
